\subsection{Performance of EHZ Capacity Computation}
\label{sec:benchmark}

The HK2017 algorithm has exponential cost in the number of facets~$F$.
We benchmark the implementation to establish practical limits for dataset
generation and to quantify the growth rate.

\subsubsection*{Setup}

We use the main polytope dataset (Section~\ref{sec:systolic-ratios}): 337
random 4-polytopes across facet counts~$F = 5, \ldots, 14$ generated by
rejection sampling (heights in~$[0.5, 2.0]$), with 50 samples each
at~$F = 5$--$10$, decreasing to 2 at~$F = 14$. Each polytope's EHZ capacity
was computed with \texttt{ehz\_capacity\_pruned} in release mode, after the
optimizations described in Section~\ref{sec:optimization}.

\subsubsection*{Exponential model}

A log-linear regression on the median times yields the model
\[
  T(F) \;=\; 7.3 \times 10^{-8} \cdot 4.76^F \quad\text{seconds}
  \qquad (R^2 = 0.990).
\]
The growth rate of~$4.76\times$ per facet is consistent with the combinatorial
explosion: the number of cyclic permutations of a facet subset grows
super-exponentially with~$F$, and adjacency pruning removes a roughly constant
fraction of branches at each level.

Figure~\ref{fig:benchmark-timing} shows the data and fitted model.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{../experiments/figures/benchmark_timing.png}
\caption{EHZ capacity computation time vs facet count for 337 random polytopes.
  Diamonds: median per facet count. Red line: fitted exponential model.}
\label{fig:benchmark-timing}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection*{Practical limits}

Based on the model:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $F \le 8$: sub-25\,ms, suitable for large datasets (1000+ polytopes).
  \item $F = 9$--$10$: 58--267\,ms median, feasible for 100--500 polytopes.
  \item $F = 11$: $\sim$1.6\,s median, feasible for 20--50 polytopes.
  \item $F = 12$: $\sim$9\,s median, feasible for 10--20 polytopes.
  \item $F = 13$: $\sim$44\,s median, feasible for 5--10 polytopes.
  \item $F = 14$: $\sim$9\,min median, feasible for 1--5 polytopes.
  \item $F = 16$: $\sim$3.4\,hr (projected), single-run only.
  \item $F \ge 18$: days per polytope.
\end{itemize}

The 16-facet crosspolytope (the smallest known counterexample candidate after
the HK-O pentagon) requires exploring all subsets of 16 facets. While the
per-iteration cost has been reduced (Section~\ref{sec:optimization}), the
combinatorial explosion at~$F = 16$ remains prohibitive for brute-force
computation.
